rv.q: In the end, boldness and idiosyncrasy make this production compelling and confusing in equal measure.
And that is a good reason to go along and see this revival.
But amid the bluster and gimmick of the staging, Caryl Churchill’s swipe at colonialism and fierce exploration of modern sexuality feels a little less impactful in this ambitious but uneven revival.

cn.t: Churchill's satire feels dated to modern audiences, though critics appreciate its bold theatricality and a riotous first act that outshines a weaker second half.
